We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 3} 2^{(-2x+4)}} &= 2^{(-2(3)+4)}\\[5pt] &= 2^{(-2)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2^2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align*}

We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^x + 2}{2^x + 3} &= \dfrac{\lim_\limits{x \to 0}\left(e^x + 2\right)}{\lim_\limits{x \to 0}\left(2^x + 3\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^0 + 2}{2^0 + 3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 + 2}{1 + 3}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{4}} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
We can use the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

\begin{align*} \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{7e^{3x-8}}{3} &= \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(\dfrac{7}{3} \cdot e^{3x} \cdot e^{-8}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{7e^{-8}}{3} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} e^{3x} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Next, we recall the graph of $y = e^{3x}.$

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ decreases. Therefore, \[ \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} e^{3x} = 0. \]

We conclude that \[ \dfrac{7e^{-8}}{3} \cdot \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} e^{3x} = \dfrac{7e^{-8}}{3} \cdot 0 = 0. \]

question.explanation:
First, we rewrite the limit as follows:

\begin{align*} \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^{-5x} &= \lim_{x\to -\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^{5x}\\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to -\infty} \left[\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^{5}\right]^x\\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to -\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 {32}\right)^x \end{align*}

Next, we recall the graph of $y = \left(\dfrac 1 {32}\right)^x.$

From the graph, we see that the function increases without bound as $x$ decreases. Therefore,

\[ \lim_{x\to -\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 {32}\right)^{x} = \infty. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ \lim_{x\to -\infty} 2^{-5x} = \infty. \]
